questions.question: If an aircraft is loaded so that the aft C.G. limit is exceeded, what undesirable flight characteristic is likely to result?
questions.idealAnswer: The aircraft will be tail-heavy and may be unable to recover from a stall or spin.

questions.question: If all the records for an aircraft are missing, how would you determine the empty weight and empty weight C.G.?
questions.idealAnswer: The aircraft would have to be weighed, and new weight and balance records would have to be prepared.

questions.question: Define “tare weight” and describe how it is handled when weighing an aircraft.
questions.idealAnswer: Tare weight is the weight of anything on the scales that is not part of the aircraft. It must be subtracted from the scale weight reading to determine the net weight of the airplane.

questions.question: If a piece of equipment such as a radio is added to an aircraft, how can you determine the effect on weight and balance without re-weighing the aircraft?
questions.idealAnswer: If the weight and balance records are up to date, a new weight and C.G. location can be determined by computation.

questions.question: Why is control of the weight and balance of an aircraft important?
questions.idealAnswer: To provide maximum safety.

questions.question: What is the datum of an aircraft and what is its function?
questions.idealAnswer: The datum is an imaginary vertical plane at right angles to the longitudinal axis of the airplane. It is the reference point from which all horizontal measurements are taken.

concepts.label: Imaginary vertical plane right angles longitudinal axis airplane
terms: imaginary vertical plane right angles longitudinal axis airplane

conceptGroups.label: Imaginary vertical plane right angles longitudinal axis airplane
acceptedTerms: imaginary vertical plane right angles longitudinal axis airplane

questions.question: How do you determine the moment of an item of equipment?
questions.idealAnswer: The weight of the item is multiplied by its arm, which is the distance between the item and the datum.

questions.question: What are two ways of determining the arm of an item of equipment?
questions.idealAnswer: Measure the distance between the item and the datum, or use data supplied by the manufacturer.

questions.question: What should be done to obtain a positive (plus) moment aft of the datum?
questions.idealAnswer: Add weight.

questions.question: What should be done to obtain a negative (minus) moment aft of the datum?
questions.idealAnswer: Remove weight.

questions.question: What should be done to obtain a positive (plus) moment forward of the datum?
questions.idealAnswer: Remove weight.

questions.question: What should be done to obtain a negative (minus) moment forward of the datum?
questions.idealAnswer: Add weight.

questions.question: How does the category of an aircraft affect its loaded weight?
questions.idealAnswer: Aircraft certificated in more than one category, such as Normal and Aerobatic, may have two different maximum gross weights and different useful loads.

concepts.label: Certificated one normal aerobatic two different maximum gross different useful loads

questions.question: As you prepare an aircraft for weighing, you determine that there is equipment aboard that is not permanently installed and recorded on the equipment list. What should you do with this equipment?
questions.idealAnswer: All equipment not permanently installed in the aircraft or included on the equipment list should be removed from the aircraft.

questions.question: Define the term “residual fuel.”.
questions.idealAnswer: Any fuel that remains in the tanks, lines, and engines, after the system has been drained.

questions.question: Define the term “residual oil.”.
questions.idealAnswer: Any oil that remains in the tanks, lines, and engines, after the system has been drained.

questions.question: How should you account for fuel when weighing an aircraft to determine weight and balance?
questions.idealAnswer: Either drain the fuel system until only unusable fuel remains, or fill the tanks full and subtract out the weight of the useable fuel.

questions.question: Where are leveling instructions found, and describe one method of leveling an aircraft?
questions.idealAnswer: Leveling instructions are found in the Type Certificate Data Sheets. An aircraft may be leveled by using a spirit level at specified points, or an aircraft may be leveled by using a plumb bob from a designated point along with a leveling scale or protractor.

questions.question: Define the term “Mean Aerodynamic Chord” or MAC.
questions.idealAnswer: Mean Aerodynamic Chord is the chord drawn through the center of the wing plan area.

questions.question: Describe the two most common ways of showing the C.G. location and/or C.G. range.
questions.idealAnswer: In inches from the datum or in percent of MAC.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an aircraft loading graph?
questions.idealAnswer: It is a method for determining how to distribute the load so as to keep the C.G. within allowable limits.

questions.idealAnswer: Ballast may be installed in the tail to move the C.G. aft.

questions.question: How does the C.G. range of a helicopter compare to that of a fixed-wing airplane?
questions.idealAnswer: Helicopters typically have a much smaller C.G. range.

questions.question: When computing weight and balance, what is the "moment" and how is it obtained?
questions.idealAnswer: Moment is a force which tends to rotate the aircraft about one of its axes. It is obtained by multiplying the weight of an item (pounds) by the distance of the item from the datum (inches). It is expressed in "inch-pounds." (W x A = M)

questions.question: What is the "arm" of an item and how is it obtained?
questions.idealAnswer: The arm is the distance (in inches) an item is located either forward or aft of the datum. It is obtained either by actual measurement or from the aircraft weight and balance records.

questions.question: What is meant by "minimum fuel" and how is it calculated for weight and balance?
questions.idealAnswer: The amount of fuel needed for an extreme condition check, to see if the center of gravity will be out of limits in that situation. For a reciprocating engine airplane, the calculation is: maximum except takeoff horsepower divided by two (METO divided by 2).

questions.idealAnswer: It is the distance in inches from the most forward acceptable center of gravity to the most rearward acceptable center of gravity.

questions.question: Where is the center of gravity located in relation to the aerodynamic center of lift for most airplanes?

questions.question: If the forward C.G. Limit of an aircraft is exceeded after installing several items in the engine compartment, how could the limit be returned to limits without removing or changing any of the newly installed equipment?
questions.idealAnswer: By adding a ballast weight in the rear of the aircraft.

questions.question: What are the placard requirements for ballast?
questions.idealAnswer: The ballast location must have a placard stating any limitations on contents, including weight, that are necessary under the loading requirements.

questions.question: What is recommended for marking of permanent ballast?
questions.idealAnswer: In red paint, mark with "permanent ballast, do not remove."

questions.question: How can you determine if a part will affect the CG without weighing the aircraft?
questions.idealAnswer: The effect can be determined by basic computations if the weight and balance records are up to date. If the records are up to date, basic weight and balance computations may be used.
